subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: Show that 1/(3x + 1) + 1/(x + 1) − 1/((3x + 1)(x + 1)) does not lie between 1 and 4, if x is real.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.54 (PDF p.55 — in this region of the scan the offset is book + 1, not the book + 2 that docs/IPE_MATHS_2A_SOURCE.md states; the page number printed on the page is the authority) — SAQ chapter 8 Quadratic Expressions, answer 66. Printed appearances: AP 15,16,17,19 · TS 16,18,22. ⚠ THE 1+1+1+1 SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed anywhere on book pp.52–54. It follows the four moves an examiner ticks in this method: form the quadratic in x · write Δ ≥ 0 · solve the inequality in y · state the range. The SAME split and the SAME step ids (s1_quadratic_in_x, s2_discriminant, s3_solve_in_y, s4_range) are used on all five range / maximum / lies-between SAQs in this unit (answers 63.1, 63.2, 64, 65, 66), deliberately: they are one method — cross-multiply, quadratic in x, discriminant ≥ 0, solve the inequality in y — over different numbers. The book's SAQ chapter header carries ★★★ and reads '4 Marks'; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-2A Section B runs Q11–Q17 at 4 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q12 is the Quadratic Expressions slot (blueprint, book p.3, and all five model papers, book pp.111–120). This question is re-solved as the third Q12 item of the Bullet Model Paper (book p.101) with the same result; it does not appear in the five model papers. No two-book check and no board back-test exist for this paper — there is no second Maths-2A source in the corpus and answer-book/papers/ holds first-year physics only — recorded, not hidden. Note on the domain: x = −1 and x = −1/3 make a denominator zero and are excluded. The card checks that neither is ever a root of the quadratic in x (substituting gives 3 and 1/3, never 0), so the discriminant argument introduces no false value of y; the book does not mention this.

recall_prompt: Say how you would show the expression never lies between 1 and 4 — say how you simplify it first, what you call y, what equation in x you form, what condition x being real gives, and how the conclusion comes out.
insider_note: Combine the three fractions first — the common denominator is already there and the numerator reduces to one linear term. 'Does not lie between' reverses the range habit: the product is ≥ 0, so y lies OUTSIDE the two values, and writing the between-answer proves the opposite of the claim.

steps.label: Quadratic in x
steps.margin_note: First mark, and it has two parts: simplify, THEN set y. The common denominator is already (3x + 1)(x + 1); the numerator is (x + 1) + (3x + 1) − 1 = 4x + 1. Only then cross-multiply. x = −1 and x = −1/3 are excluded (denominator zero); neither is ever a root of (1), so nothing false enters.
lines: (1) is a quadratic in x, and x is real.

recall.must_convey: That the three fractions are first combined over the common denominator (3x + 1)(x + 1) to (4x + 1)/(3x² + 4x + 1), then set equal to y and collected into the quadratic 3yx² + (4y − 4)x + (y − 1) = 0.
accept: let y equal the expression, cross multiply and collect terms to get a quadratic in x
put y equal to the fraction, multiply out the denominator and write it as a quadratic in x
call the expression y and rearrange it into a x squared plus b x plus c equals zero
first add the three fractions over the common denominator to get four x plus one over three x squared plus four x plus one then let that be y
expression ni y ani pettukoni cross multiply chesi x lo quadratic rayali

steps.why: The discriminant method needs ONE fraction. Combining first turns a three-term expression into the standard shape, and the rest of the question is then identical to every other range question.
common_mistakes: Cross-multiplying each fraction separately instead of combining them first.
Getting the numerator as 4x + 2 by forgetting the −1.
Not writing that (1) is a quadratic in x with x real.

steps.label: Δ ≥ 0
steps.margin_note: Second mark. a = 3y, b = 4y − 4, c = y − 1. (4y − 4)² = 16y² − 32y + 16 and 4(3y)(y − 1) = 12y² − 12y, subtracted. Here the leading coefficient comes out POSITIVE, so no sign flip is needed later.

recall.must_convey: That x real gives Δ ≥ 0: (4y − 4)² − 4(3y)(y − 1) ≥ 0, which simplifies to 4y² − 20y + 16 ≥ 0.
accept: x is real so the discriminant b squared minus four a c must be greater than or equal to zero
the quadratic in x has real roots so delta is at least zero
apply b squared minus 4 a c greater than or equal to zero to the quadratic in x
x real kabatti delta greater than or equal to zero pettali
heard_as: b squared minus four a c
greater than or equal to zero
four y squared minus twenty y

steps.why: x is real, so the quadratic (1) has a real root and its discriminant is at least zero. This time the resulting quadratic in y opens upward, which is why the answer is the OUTSIDE of two roots.
common_mistakes: Writing 4(3y)(y − 1) as 12y² − 12 (the 12y term needs the y).
Using Δ > 0, which mis-handles the boundary values 1 and 4.

steps.label: Solve for y
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Dividing by the positive number 4 keeps the inequality as it is. A product ≥ 0 means y is OUTSIDE the roots — y ≤ 1 or y ≥ 4 — the opposite of the range questions, and exactly what 'does not lie between' needs.

recall.must_convey: That dividing by 4 gives y² − 5y + 4 ≥ 0, which factorises as (y − 1)(y − 4) ≥ 0, so y ≤ 1 or y ≥ 4 — the OUTSIDE of the roots.
accept: multiply by minus one to make the leading coefficient positive, factorise and read off the interval for y
factorise the quadratic in y and find where the product is less than or equal to zero
solve the quadratic inequality in y by factoring
divide by four and factorise as y minus one into y minus four greater than or equal to zero so y is outside one and four
y lo quadratic inequality ni factorise chesi y ki interval teeyali
heard_as: less than or equal to one
greater than or equal to four

steps.why: Inside or outside depends on the sign of the leading coefficient. It is positive here, and the inequality is ≥, so y is outside the two roots; that is the whole content of the claim.
common_mistakes: Writing 1 ≤ y ≤ 4 by habit from the range questions.
Dividing by 4 and reversing the inequality — only a NEGATIVE divisor reverses it.

steps.label: Range
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The values 1 and 4 themselves ARE reached (Δ = 0 there: y = 1 at x = 0, y = 4 at x = −1/2); the claim is about the open gap between them, and that gap is empty. End with the question's own sentence.
lines: So no value of y lies strictly between 1 and 4.

lines.text: ∴ y does not lie between 1 and 4

recall.must_convey: That y is never strictly between 1 and 4, so the expression does not lie between 1 and 4 — the statement to be shown.
accept: so y never lies between one and four which is what we had to show
the expression is either at most one or at least four so it does not lie between one and four
no value of the expression is between one and four hence shown
y one ki four ki madhya undadu, so expression does not lie between one and four
hence the expression does not lie between one and four

steps.why: A 'show that' question is complete only when the required statement is written as the conclusion. 'y ≤ 1 or y ≥ 4' is that statement in symbols; the sentence is it in words.
common_mistakes: Ending at y ≤ 1 or y ≥ 4 without the sentence.
Claiming y is never equal to 1 or 4 — both values are reached.
Concluding 'lies between 1 and 4' by mis-reading the direction of the inequality.
